thread.title: Trading Mistake 8 (Apple): Poor Profit-Taking - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Individual Trader
title: Trading Mistake 8 (Apple): Poor Profit-Taking - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Fear and greed are what run the stock market. Trader A buys a stock, makes a decent paper profit over a short time frame and becomes fearful of losing those gains. He ponders to himself - " How can I let these profits go especially considering the time-frame I made them in". He continues - " If I was able to make these gains so fast - I could lose them as a fast also". What eventually happens to the trader with this mindset ? Well you can bet that he will be out on the first down-tick. The "fear of loss" mindset was what drove him to it.
However let's take this one step further. Who bought the stock off him ? What does the latter trader see that the former didn't when he sold. In fact, I bet the initial trader spent so much time researching that long play, perfected a great entry only to literally puke up his shares once the shares came into a tiny bit of profit. Trader or Investor B didn't care about an exact entry and may have a totally different outlook with respect how long he is going to hold the shares. When swing trading, our time-frame goal is usually 1 to 3 months depending on volatility. But how do we ensure that we don't let a good trade get out of our hands for a minuscule profit?
From a personal point of view, knowing when to take profits is definitely one of the most difficult skills to master. I wrote in an previous article that one's mindset should be to never let a winning trade turn around into a losing one. I acknowledge this is difficult when one doesn't get a strong trending move in the trade initially.
In this article, I will use Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL ) as the test case. As the chart illustrates below, Apple has been an excellent trading vehicle over the past year or so. Every time sentiment got ultra pessimistic which many times corresponded with oversold momentum indicators, the stock formed a bottom and quickly rallied to the upside.
Furthermore from a fundamental standpoint, there was nothing in the company's recent second quarter earnings to suggest that growth could be finished here. In fact, shares have been on a tear since the earnings release as the second quarter saw a cool 14% spike in iPhone revenue despite the fact that only 3% growth was registered in the actual phones. This demonstrates the strength of the iPhone brand & the pricing power the company is still able to garner from its customers. The other product segments grew by almost 40% on a rolling year basis and service revenue grew by just over 30%. Currently though with Apple trading at just over $187 a share, we are looking at cash flow multiple of 14.4 and a sales multiple of 3.9. Both of these valuation metrics are meaningfully higher than Apple's 5 year averages. Therefore, for anyone buying on dips or simply swing trading Apple to the upside, the below profit taking strategy may help in some way.
Source: Sentimentrader.com
At the way sentiment is dropping, I don't know if shares are going to make it all the way back to the 200 day moving average ($167) before the next buy signal materializes. Therefore let's say the next prime buying opportunity occurs at the present 50 day average at around $175 a share. This may never happen due to the stock taking out its all time highs. However for the purpose of this article, we would obviously wait for a swing low before entering the trade.
Lets say 200 shares are bought at the $175 price which would mean an investment of $35,000. One obviously could also buy call options as AAPL is a highly liquid stock meaning the bid/ask spreads are very tight. This enables one to get in and out at favorable prices not like other underylings whose options have very poor liquidity.
For the purpose of this article though, we will stick to our 20 shares or $3,500 investment. From the obvious benefit of hindsight, here is how I would trade AAPL from the long side at present.
The major swings this year have resulted in at least a 20%+ move from lows to highs in this stock. These meaningful moves took place in February & May. If we were lucky enough to enter at $175, our strategy would be to take 50% of our profits once AAPL moves 10% off these lows or to the $192.50 level. Our profit would be $3500 (10% of $35,000) so 50% or $1750 would be the amount we would take off the table at this juncture. This $1750 is money banked , which means it cannot be lost which we will explain. This is step 1. This means we still have $36,750 still in play. So how do we make sure that our $1750 is the minimum we will make on this trade? What we do is place a stop loss at precisely the same time we booked the initial 50% profit of $1750. Something like 4 to 5% to enable the position maybe work off some short term overbought conditions. So since we have $36,750 at play, we could put a wide stop loss to stop out of our AAPL shares once their value hits $35,000 or above ( your initial investment). Here we are at least making what we banked originally - the initial $1750 if the worst case scenario transpired and our stop got hit. However let's say our wide stop loss didn't get hit and Apple rallies another 10%. Now our investment has increased to $40,425. We notice that sentiment is getting lofty and the RSI momentum indicators are becoming severely overbought. Most traders would take full profits here but we don't want to do that. Tech is still in a roaring bull market and is one of the leading sectors of this equity bull run. We would probably take $1425 profit out of the trade and push up the stop loss to the $3,700 mark. So now we have banked $1750 + $1425 ($3175) and have moved our stop loss up to $37,000 which if gets hit would be another $2000 profit on the trade. So let's tie this all together. Just say our $37,000 stop loss finally gets hit. This means we made $1750+$1425+$2000 on the trade. This gives us a grand total of $5175 profit. Our original investment was $3,500 which means we recorded a 14.8% gain. Now the max gain we could have made on this hypothetical example was 20% if we got out at the very top so yes because of our trade management, we lost just over 5%. This figure assumes we would have been able to get out at the very top which is a really difficult skill. However, here is the skinny which is vital for swing traders. When one consistently takes profits off the table on the way up, you are doing two things. You are banking profits and also putting yourself in a position where you can place a lower stop loss ( that you would have had if you still had all of your initial shares) which keeps you in the game for longer. This really is the skinny of this article. I've made so many mistakes either taking full profits too early or letting all my profits slide. This strategy does away with all that. Furthermore, it is an excellent strategy for stocks in bull mode but with pricey valuations like we have at the moment in tech.
Have the courage to hold a swing trade for the time you think it needs. Chip away at the profit (especially on the initial move) on the upside and bank those profits. Don't be afraid of profits disappearing. Patience is not simply the ability to wait - it's how we behave while we're waiting.
